claim: Conserved peptides encoded by mille-pattes (mlpt)/polished rice (pri)/tarsal less (tal) are essential for embryo segmentation in Tribolium.
source: Conserved peptides encoded by mille-pattes (mlpt)/polished rice (pri)/tarsal less (tal) are essential for embryo segmentation in Tribolium but, in Drosophila, function in terminal epidermal differentiation and patterning of adult legs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Savard et al., 2006) and experimental data presented in the manuscript showing segmentation defects in Tribolium upon mlpt knockdown.

claim: In Drosophila, mlpt/pri/tal peptides function in terminal epidermal differentiation and patterning of adult legs.
source: Conserved peptides encoded by mille-pattes (mlpt)/polished rice (pri)/tarsal less (tal) are essential for embryo segmentation in Tribolium but, in Drosophila, function in terminal epidermal differentiation and patterning of adult legs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Galindo et al., 2007; Kondo et al., 2007) and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: A molecular complex comprising Mlpt peptides, ubiquitin-ligase Ubr3 and transcription factor Shavenbaby (Svb) was identified in Drosophila epidermal differentiation.
source: Here, we show that a molecular complex identified in Drosophila epidermal differentiation, comprising Mlpt peptides, ubiquitin-ligase Ubr3 and transcription factor Shavenbaby (Svb), represents an ancient developmental module required for early insect embryo patterning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kondo et al., 2010; Zanet et al., 2015) describing the molecular interactions between these components.

claim: The Mlpt/Ubr3/Svb complex represents an ancient developmental module required for early insect embryo patterning.
source: Here, we show that a molecular complex identified in Drosophila epidermal differentiation, comprising Mlpt peptides, ubiquitin-ligase Ubr3 and transcription factor Shavenbaby (Svb), represents an ancient developmental module required for early insect embryo patterning.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing conserved function across multiple insect species (Tribolium, Oncopeltus, Gerris, Nasonia).

claim: Loss of segmentation function for the Mlpt/Ubr3/Svb module in flies evolved concomitantly with restriction of Svb expression in early Drosophila embryos.
source: We find that loss of segmentation function for this module in flies evolved concomitantly with restriction of Svb expression in early Drosophila embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that svb expression is absent in the early Drosophila embryo abdomen, unlike in other insects examined, and by expression pattern comparisons across species.

claim: Artificially restoring early Svb expression in flies causes segmentation defects that depend on mlpt function.
source: Consistent with this observation, artificially restoring early Svb expression in flies causes segmentation defects that depend on mlpt function, demonstrating enduring potency of an ancestral developmental switch despite evolving embryonic patterning modes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing segmentation defects upon ectopic svb expression in Drosophila, and rescue of these defects in mlpt mutant background.

claim: The ancestral developmental switch retains potency despite evolving embryonic patterning modes.
source: Consistent with this observation, artificially restoring early Svb expression in flies causes segmentation defects that depend on mlpt function, demonstrating enduring potency of an ancestral developmental switch despite evolving embryonic patterning modes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observation that ectopic svb expression can induce segmentation defects in Drosophila, suggesting the molecular machinery remains functional.

claim: Animal genomes transcribe a variety of long-non-coding RNAs whose functions are not yet fully understood.
source: Animal genomes transcribe a variety of long-non-coding RNAs, whose functions are not yet fully understood (Cech and Steitz, 2014; Guttman and Rinn, 2012; Perry and Ulitsky, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles discussing long non-coding RNAs.

claim: Long 'non-coding' RNAs encode 'micropeptides' from small open reading frames < 100 amino acids.
source: A large body of evidence increasingly supports translation of so called 'micropeptides' from small open reading frames < 100 amino acids (also called small ORFs, smORFs or sORFs) encoded in long 'non-coding' RNAs (Couso and Patraquim, 2017; Plaza et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature on micropeptide discovery and validation.

claim: Micropeptides represent an overlooked reservoir of evolutionary and regulatory material.
source: Owing to their relatively recent discovery and experimental validation, micropeptides represent an overlooked reservoir of evolutionary and regulatory material.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the recent discovery of micropeptides and their limited characterization to date.

claim: mlpt/tarsal less/polished rice peptides (10 to 32 amino acids) are conserved across arthropods, representing over 400 million years of evolutionary time.
source: One of the best-known cases of smORF-encoded peptides called mille-pattes/tarsal less/polished rice (10 to 32 amino acids; hereafter referred to as mlpt), are conserved across arthropods, a taxon representing over 400 million years of evolutionary time (Galindo et al., 2007; Kondo et al., 2007; Savard et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating conservation of mlpt across arthropods.

claim: Drosophila embryos lacking mlpt function develop with proper segment patterning but exhibit strong defects in epidermal differentiation, notably the absence of cuticular trichomes.
source: It has been shown that Drosophila embryos lacking mlpt function develop with proper segment patterning, but exhibit strong defects in epidermal differentiation, notably the absence of cuticular trichomes (Galindo et al., 2007; Kondo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work on Drosophila mlpt mutants.

claim: In the fly epidermis, Mlpt peptides act through post-translational control of Ovo/Shavenbaby (Svb).
source: In the fly epidermis, Mlpt peptides act through post-translational control of Ovo/Shavenbaby (Svb)(Kondo et al., 2010), a transcription factor well-established as the key regulator of trichomes (Payre et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating the molecular mechanism of Mlpt action on Svb.

claim: Svb is a transcription factor well-established as the key regulator of trichomes.
source: In the fly epidermis, Mlpt peptides act through post-translational control of Ovo/Shavenbaby (Svb)(Kondo et al., 2010), a transcription factor well-established as the key regulator of trichomes (Payre et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work establishing Svb's role in trichome formation.

claim: Svb is translated as a transcriptional repressor.
source: Svb is translated as a transcriptional repressor (Kondo et al., 2010) and Mlpt peptides bind to and activate an E3 ubiquitin ligase, Ubr3, enabling its interaction with Svb (Zanet et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work characterizing Svb protein function.

claim: Mlpt peptides bind to and activate an E3 ubiquitin ligase, Ubr3, enabling its interaction with Svb.
source: Svb is translated as a transcriptional repressor (Kondo et al., 2010) and Mlpt peptides bind to and activate an E3 ubiquitin ligase, Ubr3, enabling its interaction with Svb (Zanet et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work demonstrating the molecular interaction between Mlpt, Ubr3, and Svb.

claim: Formation of the Mlpt/Ubr3/Svb complex leads to proteasome degradation of the Svb N-terminal repression domain, releasing a shorter Svb protein that functions as a transcriptional activator.
source: Formation of the Mlpt/Ubr3/Svb complex leads to proteasome degradation of the Svb N-terminal repression domain thereby, releasing a shorter Svb protein that functions as a transcriptional activator (Kondo et al., 2010; Zanet et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating the mechanism of Svb processing and activation.

claim: Upon processing, Svb activates the expression of cellular effectors comprising a gene network deeply conserved throughout arthropods.
source: Upon processing, Svb activates the expression of cellular effectors (Chanut-Delalande et al., 2006; Fernandes et al., 2010; Menoret et al., 2013), comprising a gene network deeply conserved throughout arthropods (Chanut-Delalande et al., 2006; Li et al., 2016; Spanier et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work identifying Svb target genes and their conservation.

claim: A central function of Mlpt peptides during Drosophila development is to provide temporal control of Svb transcriptional activity.
source: Hence, a central function of Mlpt peptides during Drosophila development is to provide temporal control of Svb transcriptional activity, exemplified by their role in epidermal differentiation (Chanut-Delalande et al., 2014; Zanet et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents a synthesis of the molecular mechanism described.

claim: RNAi knockdown of mlpt in Tribolium castaneum caused posterior truncation of the embryo with a loss of abdominal segments and transformation of remaining anterior abdominal segments to thoracic fate.
source: In beetles, RNAi knockdown of mlpt caused posterior truncation of the embryo, with a loss of abdominal segments, as well as the transformation of remaining anterior abdominal segments to thoracic fate, leading to a distinctive phenotype of extra pairs of legs (mille-pattes is French for centipede).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Savard et al., 2006) and is consistent with data presented in the manuscript.

claim: mlpt acts as a gap gene in Tribolium.
source: Additional work established that mlpt acts as a gap gene in Tribolium (Boos et al., 2018; Ribeiro et al., 2017; Savard et al., 2006; van der Zee et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2017), where more limited homeotic transformations often accompany loss of gap gene function (Bucher and Klingler, 2004; Cerny et al., 2005; Marques-Souza et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work characterizing mlpt function in Tribolium.

claim: Drosophila has evolved a derived mode of segmentation called 'long germ' in which all segments are formed nearly simultaneously in the syncytial environment of the blastoderm.
source: Unlike Drosophila which has evolved a derived mode of segmentation (called 'long germ') in which all segments are formed nearly simultaneously in the syncytial environment of the blastoderm, Tribolium is more representative of the ancestral mode of segmentation in insects (Peel et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and represents established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: Tribolium is more representative of the ancestral mode of segmentation in insects.
source: Unlike Drosophila which has evolved a derived mode of segmentation (called 'long germ') in which all segments are formed nearly simultaneously in the syncytial environment of the blastoderm, Tribolium is more representative of the ancestral mode of segmentation in insects (Peel et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on insect segmentation evolution.

claim: Most insects develop as short/intermediate germband embryos where only head and thorax are patterned in the blastoderm, whereas most or all posterior segments are added from a posterior 'growth zone'.
source: Most insects, like beetles, develop as short/intermediate germband embryos where only head and thorax are patterned in the blastoderm, whereas most or all posterior segments are added from a posterior 'growth zone' (Davis and Patel, 2002; Liu and Kaufman, 2005; Rosenberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on insect embryonic development.

claim: The genome-wide iBeetle RNAi screen in Tribolium allowed a large-scale search for patterning genes leading to a mlpt-like mutant phenotype.
source: The genome-wide iBeetle RNAi screen in Tribolium (Dönitz et al., 2018; Dönitz et al., 2015; Schmitt-Engel et al., 2015) allowed a large-scale search for patterning genes leading to a mlpt-like mutant phenotype, as a means of identifying candidate partners.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach used and is supported by citations to the iBeetle screen publications.

claim: Knockdown of Tc-ubr3 in Tribolium phenocopies mlpt RNAi with severely shortened larvae due to the absence of many abdominal segments as well as telson appendages.
source: In Tribolium, the Tc-ubr3 RNAi phenocopies mlpt RNAi with severely shortened larvae due to the absence of many abdominal segments as well as telson appendages (Figure 1A–C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: In Tc-ubr3 RNAi, the remaining 'abdominal' segments appear to be transformed to a thoracic fate since they bear extra legs and often spiracles resembling those present on the second thoracic segment.
source: Furthermore, as in mlpt RNAi, the remaining 'abdominal' segments appear to be transformed to a thoracic fate since they bear extra legs and often spiracles resembling those present on the second thoracic segment (Figure 1A–C and Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: The Tc-Ubr3 phenotype can exceed mlpt RNAi in severity, with strongly affected legs developing shorter and poorly differentiated segments.
source: The Tc-Ubr3 phenotype can exceed mlpt RNAi in severity, with strongly affected legs developing shorter and poorly differentiated segments (Figure 1F,G and Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: The overall similarity between mlpt and Tc-Ubr3 phenotypes suggested that the complete fly epidermal module may be conserved for Tribolium segmentation.
source: However, the overall similarity between mlpt and Tc-Ubr3 phenotypes (Table 1) suggested that the complete fly epidermal module may be conserved for Tribolium segmentation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the phenotypic similarity data presented in Table 1.

claim: Tc-Ubr3 is expressed ubiquitously in the beetle embryo.
source: As in flies, Tc-Ubr3 is expressed ubiquitously in the beetle embryo, as expected for an enzyme with additional widespread functions, including in DNA repair (Meisenberg et al., 2012) and apoptosis (Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation and citations to prior work on Ubr3 functions.

claim: Tc-svb and mlpt display a dynamic pattern during both blastoderm and germband stages of Tribolium embryogenesis.
source: In contrast, Tc-svb and mlpt display a dynamic pattern during both blastoderm and germband stages of Tribolium embryogenesis (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: Tc-svb is co-expressed with mlpt within the pre-growth zone at the onset of gastrulation.
source: Importantly, Tc-svb is co-expressed with mlpt within the pre-growth zone at the onset of gastrulation (Figure 2B,B').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: As the Tribolium embryo extends, Tc-svb forms two distinct expression domains flanking the strong mlpt expression domain.
source: As the embryo extends, Tc-svb forms two distinct expression domains flanking the strong mlpt expression domain (Figure 2D,D'), suggesting that high levels of mlpt and Tc-svb expression may be mutually repressive (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: High levels of mlpt and Tc-svb expression may be mutually repressive.
source: As the embryo extends, Tc-svb forms two distinct expression domains flanking the strong mlpt expression domain (Figure 2D,D'), suggesting that high levels of mlpt and Tc-svb expression may be mutually repressive (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the complementary expression patterns observed in Figure 2.

claim: RNAi knockdown of Tc-svb leads to a highly penetrant abdominal truncation and homeotic transformation phenotype that resembles that of mlpt and Tc-ubr3 knockdowns.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we found that RNAi knockdown of Tc-svb also leads to a highly penetrant abdominal truncation and homeotic transformation phenotype that resembles that of mlpt and Tc-ubr3 knockdowns (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Knockdown Tc-svb larvae are characterized by the presence of legs on the first two 'abdominal' segments.
source: Knockdown Tc-svb larvae are characterized by the presence of legs on the first two 'abdominal' segments, even in the weaker segmentation phenotypes, wherein legs on segment 'A1' are often reduced to mere stumps (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Presence of T2-like spiracles on 'A1' and the absence of spiracles on 'A2' in Tc-svb knockdowns suggest their transformation into thoracic segments, T2 and T3, respectively.
source: Presence of T2-like spiracles on 'A1' and the absence of spiracles on 'A2' in Tc-svb knockdowns suggest their transformation into thoracic segments, T2 and T3, respectively.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed spiracle patterns in Tc-svb knockdown larvae.

claim: In Tc-svb knockdowns, leg segments are severely shortened and rounded, and pretarsi are reduced.
source: As with mlpt and Tc-ubr3 knockdown, leg segments are severely shortened and rounded, and pretarsi are reduced in Tc-svb knockdowns (Figure 1F,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Tc-ubr3, mlpt, and Tc-svb larvae share several critical similarities, including some degree of posterior truncation, transformation of remaining abdominal segments towards thoracic identity, shortened leg segments with a 'bubble-like' terminus, and missing telson appendages.
source: In summary, in spite of some phenotypic differences, Tc-ubr3, mlpt, and Tc-svb larvae share several critical similarities, including some degree of posterior truncation, transformation of remaining abdominal segments towards thoracic identity, shortened leg segments with a 'bubble-like' terminus, and missing telson appendages (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data summarized in Table 1.

claim: A Tc-svb CRISPR mutant phenocopies the observed RNAi defects.
source: CRISPR knockout of Tc-svb phenocopies the observed RNAi defects (Figure 1A–E), and highlights an additional phenotype consisting of a considerable thinning of the epidermal cuticle, similar to what has been observed in the fly (Andrew and Baker, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and citation to prior work.

claim: Tc-svb CRISPR mutants exhibit a considerable thinning of the epidermal cuticle, similar to what has been observed in the fly.
source: CRISPR knockout of Tc-svb phenocopies the observed RNAi defects (Figure 1A–E), and highlights an additional phenotype consisting of a considerable thinning of the epidermal cuticle, similar to what has been observed in the fly (Andrew and Baker, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to prior work in Drosophila.

claim: Tc-Svb displays strong conservation of the protein motifs identified in flies as required for Svb processing: the maturation site and the N-terminal region bound and ubiquitinated by Ubr3.
source: Tc-Svb also displays strong conservation of the protein motifs identified in flies as required for Svb processing: the maturation site (Kondo et al., 2010) and the N-terminal region (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D–F) bound and ubiquitinated by Ubr3 to target Svb to the proteasome (Zanet et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and citations to prior work.

claim: The predicted disordered disposition pattern of Svb proteins remains strikingly conserved for Svb in Tribolium and other insects.
source: Despite rapid evolution of Svb protein sequence outside the zinc-finger region (Kumar et al., 2012), this predicted disordered disposition pattern remains strikingly conserved for Svb in Tribolium and other insects (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Examination of wg expression confirms that abdominal segments are specifically disrupted in mlpt, Tc-svb, and Tc-ubr3 RNAi embryos, while thoracic segments are formed normally.
source: Examination of the segmental marker wg confirms that abdominal segments are specifically disrupted in mlpt, Tc-svb, and Tc-ubr3 RNAi embryos, while thoracic segments are formed normally (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the short germ embryo of Tribolium, the head and the first thoracic segment form in the syncytial blastoderm, while after cellularization, subsequent segments continue to arise in a sequential manner from the posterior growth zone.
source: This is of interest since in the short germ embryo of Tribolium, the head and the first thoracic segment form in the syncytial blastoderm, while after cellularization, subsequent segments continue to arise in a sequential manner from the posterior growth zone (Liu and Kaufman, 2005; Rosenberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on Tribolium embryonic development.

claim: Patterns of mlpt and Tc-svb expression during Tribolium embryonic development are often complementary, and at times, overlapping.
source: In summary, patterns of mlpt and Tc-svb expression during Tribolium embryonic development are often complementary, and at times, overlapping.
evidence: This claim summarizes the expression pattern data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Loss of function phenotypes of mlpt, Tc-svb and Tc-ubr3 suggest that a functional module for mlpt discovered in Drosophila trichome patterning also works in concert in embryonic segmentation, leg patterning and cuticle formation in Tribolium.
source: Loss of function phenotypes of mlpt, Tc-svb and Tc-ubr3 suggest that a functional module for mlpt discovered in Drosophila trichome patterning also works in concert in embryonic segmentation, leg patterning and cuticle formation in Tribolium.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the phenotypic similarities observed across the three genes in Tribolium.

claim: mlpt and svb expression in the early hemipteran embryo are observed in strong domains at the anterior of the blastoderm embryo.
source: mlpt and svb expression in the early hemipteran embryo are observed in strong domains at the anterior of the blastoderm embryo (e.g., Oncopeltus, Figure 3A,A'), with additional posterior Of-svb expression at the future site of invagination which becomes broad expression throughout the early growth zone (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: Expression of svb and mlpt resolve into complementary/overlapping domains within the growth zone in hemipteran embryos.
source: Subsequently, expression of svb and mlpt resolve into complementary /overlapping domains within the growth zone (Figure 3B–E' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: Later expression of svb and mlpt in hemipteran species is seen in presumptive neurons in the central nervous system, as well as in the limb buds and mouth parts.
source: Later expression in both species is seen in presumptive neurons in the central nervous system, as well as in the limb buds and mouth parts (Figure 3C–F' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with a function in patterning the leg and head appendages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: RNAi against mlpt, svb, and ubr3 caused severe segmentation and patterning defects both in Gerris and Oncopeltus.
source: RNAi against each of these genes caused severe segmentation and patterning defects both in Gerris and Oncopeltus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and supplementary figures.

claim: mlpt RNAi in both Gerris and Oncopeltus resulted in the loss of posterior abdominal segments and fusion of thoracic segments, with shortened rounded legs that terminate proximal to the trunk.
source: mlpt RNAi in both Gerris and Oncopeltus resulted in the loss of posterior abdominal segments and fusion of thoracic segments, with shortened rounded legs that terminate proximal to the trunk; reduction and fusion of head appendages is also apparent ( and Figure 4—figure supplement 1,2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and supplementary figures.

claim: In Oncopeltus, severely affected mlpt RNAi embryos fail to gastrulate, resulting in an everted gut.
source: In Oncopeltus, severely affected embryos fail to gastrulate, resulting in an everted gut (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A",B").
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gb- and Of-svb RNAi resulted in the loss of abdominal segments and rounding of more distally truncated legs.
source: Gb- and Of-svb RNAi also resulted in the loss of abdominal segments and rounding of more distally truncated legs (Figure 4C,C'; G,G').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Following Gb-svb RNAi, even mildly affected prenymphs exhibited significant reduction in leg length.
source: Following Gb-svb RNAi, even mildly affected prenymphs exhibited significant reduction in leg length (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Examination of molecular markers confirmed strong defects in embryonic segmentation and appendage formation in both Gerris and Oncopeltus.
source: Examination of molecular markers confirmed strong defects in embryonic segmentation and appendage formation in both Gerris (Figure 4– figure supplement 4,5) and Oncopeltus (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 supplementary figures.

claim: ubr3 RNAi in both Gerris and Oncopeltus gave the most severe phenotype, reflecting its presumed additional functions independent of svb and mlpt.
source: ubr3 RNAi in both species gave the most severe phenotype, reflecting its presumed additional functions independent of svb and mlpt (Figure 4D,D'; H,H').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and inference about Ubr3's multiple functions.

claim: RNAi knockdown of mlpt, svb, and ubr3 in hemiptera leads to strong cuticle defects including the loss of trichomes.
source: As observed in Tribolium, RNAi, knockdown of mlpt, svb, and ubr3 in hemiptera also leads to strong cuticle defects including the loss of trichomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: Like Drosophila, Nasonia has evolved long germ embryogenesis, in which the embryo is mostly patterned in the context of the syncytial blastoderm.
source: Like Drosophila, Nasonia has evolved long germ embryogenesis, in which the embryo is mostly patterned in the context of the syncytial blastoderm, and which has evolved independently several times in the insect phylum (Liu and Kaufman, 2005; Misof et al., 2014; Rosenberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on Nasonia embryonic development.

claim: Previous work has identified the key role of maternal determinants and gap genes in Nasonia, which largely resemble that of Drosophila where most segmentation occurs in the blastoderm.
source: Previous work has identified the key role of maternal determinants and gap genes in Nasonia, which largely resemble that of Drosophila where most segmentation occurs in the blastoderm (Brent et al., 2007; Lynch et al., 2006), with some residual character of delayed segment patterning of the most posterior segments after cellularization (Rosenberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on Nasonia segmentation.

claim: In Drosophila, svb early expression is absent from posterior segments and restricted to two stripes in the head.
source: In Drosophila, whereas svb early expression is absent from posterior segments and restricted to two stripes in the head (Mével-Ninio et al., 1995) (Figure 5A,B), tal/mlpt is expressed more broadly throughout the blastoderm (Figure 5D,E) with a striped pattern evoking that of the pair-rule gene hairy (Galindo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and citations to prior work.

claim: tal/mlpt is expressed more broadly throughout the Drosophila blastoderm with a striped pattern evoking that of the pair-rule gene hairy.
source: In Drosophila, whereas svb early expression is absent from posterior segments and restricted to two stripes in the head (Mével-Ninio et al., 1995) (Figure 5A,B), tal/mlpt is expressed more broadly throughout the blastoderm (Figure 5D,E) with a striped pattern evoking that of the pair-rule gene hairy (Galindo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and citation to prior work.

claim: The absence of tal/mlpt, svb or Ubr3 does not alter segmentation in Drosophila, as deduced from analysis of mutant embryos lacking both maternal and zygotic contribution for each of the three genes.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we confirmed that the absence of tal/mlpt, svb or Ubr3 does not alter segmentation, as deduced from analysis of mutant embryos lacking both maternal and zygotic contribution for each of the three genes (Figure 5M–P and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: In Nasonia, both Nv-mlpt and Nv-svb are expressed in the early embryo, in adjacent prominent stripes at the posterior region of embryo that acts as the progenitor of the late-forming segments.
source: In contrast, in Nasonia, both Nv-mlpt and Nv-svb are expressed in the early embryo, in adjacent prominent stripes at the posterior region of embryo (Figure 5G–K) that acts as the progenitor of the late-forming segments (Rosenberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and citation to prior work.

claim: Nv-svb is also expressed in a prominent stripe in the middle of the embryo, similar to expression of the thoracic gap gene, Nv-krüppel.
source: Nv-svb is also expressed in a prominent stripe in the middle of the embryo (Figure 5G–H and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), similar to expression of the thoracic gap gene, Nv-krüppel (Brent et al., 2007), while Nv-mlpt expression has an anterior cap, and broad expression posterior to the Nv-svb domain (Figure 5J–K and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures, and citation to prior work.

claim: In both Nasonia and Drosophila, later expression of svb and mlpt after germband extension prefigures the pattern of epidermal trichomes.
source: In both Nasonia and Drosophila, later expression of svb and mlpt after germband extension prefigures the pattern of epidermal trichomes (Figure 5C,F; I,L and Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: Several Svb target genes encoding trichome effectors in flies are also expressed with a similar pattern in late Nasonia embryos.
source: Consistent with this observation, we find that several Svb target genes encoding trichome effectors in flies are also expressed with a similar pattern in late Nasonia embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: In a wide range of insects, complementary and/or overlapping expression of svb and mlpt in the embryo correlates with an essential role in embryonic segmentation.
source: Thus, in a wide range of insects, complementary and/or overlapping expression of svb and mlpt in the embryo correlates with an essential role in embryonic segmentation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the expression and functional data presented across multiple insect species.

claim: Nv-mlpt RNAi causes posterior truncation and segment fusions, evident as severely shortened larvae, with two remaining trichome belts that likely correspond to thoracic and anterior abdominal segments.
source: Nv-mlpt RNAi causes posterior truncation and segment fusions, evident as severely shortened larvae, with two remaining trichome belts that likely correspond to thoracic and anterior abdominal segments (Figure 5Q,S and Figure 5—figure supplement 5A–A'').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: Nv-svb RNAi causes severe posterior truncation and loss of most abdominal segments, with only one or two pairs of spiracles left.
source: Similarly, Nv-svb RNAi causes severe posterior truncation and loss of most abdominal segments, with only one or two pairs of spiracles left (Figure 5R and Figure 5—figure supplement 5B–B'').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: Larvae from Nv-ubr3 RNAi were almost uniformly too fragile to recover, likely owing to the observed absence/thinning of cuticle.
source: Larvae from Nv-ubr3 RNAi were almost uniformly too fragile to recover (not shown), likely owing to the observed absence/thinning of cuticle.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observation and inference about the cause of fragility.

claim: Mildly affected Nv-ubr3 RNAi larvae exhibit thin cuticle, devoid of trichomes on the posterior.
source: Mildly affected Nv-ubr3 RNAi larvae exhibit thin cuticle, devoid of trichomes on the posterior (Figure 5T and Figure 5—figure supplement 5D,D').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: The data support conserved functions for mlpt, svb and ubr3 in embryonic segmentation of Nasonia vitripennis, a long germ insect.
source: Altogether, our data support conserved functions for mlpt, svb and ubr3 in embryonic segmentation of Nasonia vitripennis, a long germ insect, leaving only Drosophila from among species tested without such an early patterning function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing segmentation defects in Nasonia upon RNAi of these genes.

claim: Ectopic expression of svb in the early Drosophila embryo (using nullo-Gal4) resulted in strong segmentation defects, with no detectable effects on tal expression.
source: Strikingly, ectopic expression of svb in the early embryo (using nullo-Gal4) resulted in strong segmentation defects, with no detectable effects on tal expression (Figure 6A–B").
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Ectopic svb expression in early Drosophila embryos dramatically increased cell death.
source: We also noticed dramatically increased cell death, as also recently reported in activation of segmentation genes (Crossman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation and citation to recent work.

claim: Similar segmentation defects were observed following maternal ectopic svb expression, albeit with stronger induction of lethality.
source: Similar defects were also observed following maternal ectopic svb expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), albeit with stronger induction of lethality.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The loss of svb expression prevents segmentation function of the trio during early embryogenesis in flies.
source: These results suggest that the loss of svb expression prevents segmentation function of the trio during early embryogenesis in flies, and thus indicates that the function of the tal/svb/ubr3 module in segmentation is contingent upon expression of all three partners.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observation that restoring svb expression causes segmentation defects.

claim: The function of the tal/svb/ubr3 module in segmentation is contingent upon expression of all three partners.
source: These results suggest that the loss of svb expression prevents segmentation function of the trio during early embryogenesis in flies, and thus indicates that the function of the tal/svb/ubr3 module in segmentation is contingent upon expression of all three partners.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that segmentation defects require both svb and tal.

claim: Expression of Svb-ACT causes segmentation defects that are reminiscent of those obtained by Svb over-expression, albeit at higher frequency.
source: When expressed in the early embryo, Svb-Act causes segmentation defects that are reminiscent of those obtained by Svb over-expression, albeit at higher frequency (Figure 6C–C").
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Expression of Svb-3Kmut, which is insensitive to Tal/Ubr3, in the early embryo did not cause segmentation defects.
source: In contrast, expression of Svb-3Kmut, which is insensitive to Tal/Ubr3, in the early embryo did not cause segmentation defects (Figure 6D–D").
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The segmentation defects observed upon Svb ectopic expression in early embryos rely on its processing into the activator form.
source: These results indicate that the segmentation defects observed upon Svb ectopic expression in early embryos rely on its processing into the activator form, and that, in this context, ectopic Svb can be regulated by endogenous Tal peptides.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of Svb-ACT and Svb-3Kmut on segmentation.

claim: Ectopic Svb can be regulated by endogenous Tal peptides in the context of early embryonic expression.
source: These results indicate that the segmentation defects observed upon Svb ectopic expression in early embryos rely on its processing into the activator form, and that, in this context, ectopic Svb can be regulated by endogenous Tal peptides.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the requirement for Tal-mediated processing for segmentation defects.

claim: The ectopic expression of Svb in the absence of tal failed to cause any detectable defects in segmentation.
source: Compared to otherwise wild-type embryos, the ectopic expression of Svb in the absence of tal failed to cause any detectable defects in segmentation (Figure 6E–G), while impaired epidermal differentiation is obvious.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The cooperativity of the mlpt/svb/ubr3 gene module has remained intact throughout evolution.
source: Taken together, these data support the conclusion that the cooperativity of this gene module has remained intact throughout evolution, and that the inactivation of its function in Drosophila segmentation involved abrogation of early expression of Svb, an essential component of the module.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that the module can still function in Drosophila when svb is expressed early.

claim: The inactivation of the module's function in Drosophila segmentation involved abrogation of early expression of Svb.
source: Taken together, these data support the conclusion that the cooperativity of this gene module has remained intact throughout evolution, and that the inactivation of its function in Drosophila segmentation involved abrogation of early expression of Svb, an essential component of the module.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the expression pattern differences and functional rescue experiments.

claim: The Mlpt/Ubr3/Svb module possesses important ancestral functions in insect embryonic segmentation.
source: Our experiments reveal how a cooperative trio of molecules, initially discovered within a more restricted capacity during terminal epidermal differentiation in Drosophila, possesses important ancestral functions in insect embryonic segmentation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional data across multiple insect species presented in the manuscript.

claim: All insects representing both ancestral and derived segmentation modes exhibit strong epidermal defects upon inactivation of any of the three functional partners (mlpt, svb, ubr3).
source: Upon the inactivation of any of the three functional partners, all insects representing both ancestral and derived segmentation modes exhibit strong epidermal defects, evident both in trichome differentiation and in the thinning of the cuticle.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data across multiple species showing cuticle and trichome defects.

claim: Several Svb epidermal targets identified in Drosophila melanogaster are similarly regulated in Tribolium.
source: Several Svb epidermal targets identified in Drosophila melanogaster (Chanut-Delalande et al., 2006; Fernandes et al., 2010; Menoret et al., 2013) and sister species (Chanut-Delalande et al., 2006) are indeed similarly regulated in Tribolium (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work showing conservation of Svb target genes.

claim: Expression patterns of Svb epidermal target genes in Nasonia support conservation of the epidermal function.
source: Expression patterns of Svb epidermal target genes in Nasonia support a similar conclusion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the expression data presented for Nasonia in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The Mlpt/Ubr3/Svb module is important for leg specification and patterning across all species examined.
source: A second shared function across all species examined is the importance of Mlpt/Ubr3/Svb for leg specification and patterning, as initially reported in flies (Galindo et al., 2007; Pueyo and Couso, 2008; Pueyo and Couso, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing leg defects across species and citations to prior work.

claim: Inactivation of any of the three partners leads to shortened and misdifferentiated legs in basal insects, often with missing/fused segments, in particular in their distal parts.
source: Analysis of more basal insects shows that inactivation of any of the three partners leads to shortened and misdifferentiated legs, often with missing/fused segments, in particular in their distal parts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing leg phenotypes across multiple species.

claim: The conserved outputs of the Mlpt/Ubr3/Svb module highlight transcriptional networks downstream of Svb whose connectivity appears largely intact over large evolutionary distances.
source: The conserved outputs of this module highlight transcriptional networks downstream of Svb whose connectivity also appears largely intact over large evolutionary distances (Spanier et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on conservation of Svb target networks.

claim: Outside of Drosophila, the module functions in the formation of posterior segments in all species tested.
source: Outside of Drosophila, we demonstrate function of the module in the formation of posterior segments in all species tested, delineating a key module for insect embryonic segmentation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing segmentation defects in Tribolium, Oncopeltus, Gerris, and Nasonia.

claim: A strong domain of svb expression in the growth zone is observed in all short germ species examined, often adjacent to a strong mlpt expression domain.
source: A strong domain of svb expression in the growth zone is observed in all short germ species examined, often adjacent to a strong mlpt expression domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data presented for Tribolium, Oncopeltus, and Gerris.

claim: In the long germ wasp embryo, Nv-mlpt and Nv-svb are expressed in adjacent/partly-overlapping domains, at the time they function in segmentation.
source: In the long germ wasp embryo, Nv-mlpt and Nv-svb are also expressed in adjacent/partly-overlapping domains, at the time they function in segmentation.
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data presented for Nasonia in Figure 5.

claim: The existence of mlpt/svb boundaries may result from mutual exclusivity between svb and mlpt expression.
source: The existence of mlpt/svb boundaries may result from mutual exclusivity between svb and mlpt expression.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed complementary expression patterns.

claim: Abutting stripes of mlpt (tal in flies) and svb have been described in formation of adult leg joints in flies.
source: Such abutting stripes of mlpt (tal in flies) and svb have been described in formation of adult leg joints in flies (Pueyo and Couso, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on leg joint formation.

claim: The Mlpt/Svb function in leg joint formation in flies involves Notch-mediated signaling.
source: It is worth mentioning that the Mlpt/Svb function in leg joint formation in flies involves Notch-mediated signaling (Pueyo and Couso, 2011), a pathway required for coordination of the segmentation clock from basal arthropods (Chipman and Akam, 2008; Eriksson et al., 2013; Stollewerk et al., 2003) to mammals (Hubaud and Pourquié, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on Notch signaling in segmentation.

claim: Svb (also known as Ovo or OvoL) is conserved in all animals, and predates bilateria.
source: Beyond insects, Svb (also known as Ovo or OvoL) is conserved in all animals, and predates bilateria (Kumar et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on Svb/Ovo evolution.

claim: Recent studies have uncovered a broader role of OvoL/Svb in epithelial organization and regulation of Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition.
source: In addition to the germline and epidermis (Dai et al., 1998; Lee et al., 2014; Nair et al., 2006), recent studies have uncovered a broader role of OvoL/Svb in epithelial organization and regulation of Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (Bai et al., 2018; Kitazawa et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2014; Nieto et al., 2016; Watanabe et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work on OvoL/Svb functions.

claim: Basal insect embryos with reduced mlpt or svb often appear deficient in convergent extension.
source: Interestingly, basal insect embryos with reduced mlpt or svb often appear deficient in convergent extension (Figure 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 4), suggesting that this module may be involved in the control of cytoskeletal rearrangement during segmentation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed morphological defects in RNAi embryos.

claim: The Mlpt/Ubr3/Svb module may be involved in the control of cytoskeletal rearrangement during segmentation.
source: Interestingly, basal insect embryos with reduced mlpt or svb often appear deficient in convergent extension (Figure 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 4), suggesting that this module may be involved in the control of cytoskeletal rearrangement during segmentation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed convergent extension defects.

claim: Multi-protein complexes appear to evolve more slowly than gene regulatory networks.
source: Multi-protein complexes appear to evolve more slowly than gene regulatory networks (Tan et al., 2007), mirroring deep conservation of protein-protein interaction domains across orthologues.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on protein complex evolution.

claim: Ubr3 is required for the activity of the Mlpt/Ubr3/Svb complex, but its function is permissive, as seen by ubiquitous expression across species.
source: Our data show that Ubr3 is required for the activity of the complex, but its function is clearly permissive, as seen by ubiquitous expression across species.
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data showing ubiquitous Ubr3 expression across species.

claim: The dynamic patterns of mlpt/tal and svb highlight the key aspect of the control of their expression.
source: In contrast, the dynamic patterns of mlpt/tal and svb highlight the key aspect of the control of their expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that expression patterns, not protein function, differ between species.

claim: Evolutionary changes in enhancers and associated trans-acting factors of mlpt and svb likely underlie evolution of their function in segmentation.
source: Evolutionary changes in enhancers and associated trans-acting factors of these two instructive members of the module likely underlie evolution of their function in segmentation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the expression pattern differences and known mechanisms of gene regulation evolution.

claim: Svb enhancers are well-documented for their modifications across Tephritidae and Drosophilidae, which are causal for the evolution of trichome pattern.
source: Svb enhancers are well-documented for their modifications across Tephritidae and Drosophilidae, which are causal for the evolution of trichome pattern (Frankel et al., 2011; Frankel et al., 2012; Khila et al., 2003; McGregor et al., 2007; Preger-Ben Noon et al., 2016; Sucena et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on Svb enhancer evolution.

claim: A similar change in promoter control of Svb expression may be sufficient to bring segment patterning potency on- or off-line in the insect embryo.
source: A similar change in promoter control of Svb expression may be sufficient to bring segment patterning potency on- or off-line in the insect embryo.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the enhancer evolution data and functional experiments.

claim: The phylogenetic distribution within insects of short/long germ modes of development implies that evolution has repeatedly sampled these modes.
source: The phylogenetic distribution within insects of short/long germ modes of development implies that evolution has repeatedly sampled these modes (Misof et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on insect phylogeny and segmentation mode evolution.

claim: Recent data support a model in which segmentation mechanisms in short and long germ insects are more similar than initially thought.
source: Recent data support a model in which segmentation mechanisms in short and long germ insects are more similar than initially thought (Benton, 2018; Clark, 2017), and mostly differ in the specifics of their timing (Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work on insect segmentation mechanisms.

claim: The data suggest one mechanism by which delayed posterior segment formation may be switched on/off via Svb/Mlpt/Ubr3.
source: Our data suggest one mechanism by which delayed posterior segment formation may be switched on/off via Svb/Mlpt/Ubr3.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the functional data showing that svb expression timing controls segmentation function.
